questions.text: QUESTION 1.1 (6 marks): Write a comprehensive paragraph to Tomorrow’s Future's board explaining why projects should be selected according to the organisation’s CURRENT and FUTURE needs. Indicate how the selected project relates to those needs.
questions.correctAnswer: Projects should support an organisation's strategy and solve real present and future needs, not be started merely because technology is available. Tomorrow’s Future has become independent but still pays St John University for student and payroll services. Bringing the systems in-house could improve control, reduce dependence on the former university and meet its ongoing student, HR, reporting and payroll needs. Selection must consider urgency, benefits, risk, budget and available skills: the institution has never developed an IT project internally. Student administration or payroll could be prioritised when the institution shows how its chosen system serves both today's operations and longer-term growth.
aiRubric: Explain that project selection follows organisational strategy and current business needs.
Link future growth, flexibility and sustainability to the choice.
Identify dependence on St John University and service/billing costs.
Identify the student-system and payroll needs of the institution.
Explain how the chosen project addresses at least one of these needs.
Acknowledge feasibility: budget, risk, expertise and stakeholder input.

questions.context:
Tomorrow’s Future is a School of Graduate Leadership that used to be part of St John University. It is now independent, but St John University's computer centre still manages its staff payroll, payslips and student system, and bills Tomorrow’s Future for these services.
Management wants to take over its student system and staff salary/payroll processing in-house. It is undecided whether to buy off-the-shelf software or develop the systems itself. Some managers believe buying a package is cheaper; others disagree.
If the institution develops software in-house, these will be its first IT projects. Its IT team wants to work closely with the relevant departments, show parts of the system as they are developed, and allow changes to requirements when needed.

questions.text: QUESTION 1.2 (6 marks): Discuss ANY SIX techniques Tomorrow’s Future's project management team could use to identify potential risks for the project chosen in Question 1.1.
questions.correctAnswer: Six valid risk-identification techniques include: (1) brainstorming with the IT team and users; (2) interviewing subject experts and stakeholders; (3) the Delphi technique for independent expert input; (4) checklists or review of risks on similar projects; (5) SWOT analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats; (6) assumption and constraint analysis. Other valid methods include document review, cause-and-effect diagrams, flowcharts and lessons learned. For this case, example risks include limited in-house experience, integration, data migration, security, cost and requirement changes.
aiRubric: Credit up to six distinct recognised risk-identification techniques, ideally with brief explanation.
Brainstorming.
Interviews / expert judgement.
Delphi technique.
Checklist / historical project review.
SWOT analysis.
Assumption analysis, document review or diagramming may substitute.
Do not require these exact six or count repeated techniques twice.

questions.text: QUESTION 2.2 (5 marks): Recommend and discuss an appropriate software product-development life cycle for Tomorrow’s Future if it builds one of these systems in-house. Justify your answer using the case study.
questions.correctAnswer: An iterative/incremental or Agile development life cycle, such as Scrum supported by prototyping, suits the case. The IT team can build small working parts of the student or payroll system, demonstrate them to the relevant department, receive ongoing feedback and change requirements in later iterations. The organisation has uncertain requirements and no previous in-house IT projects, so early feedback and risk reduction are valuable. Plan releases, testing, security and integration carefully, especially for sensitive payroll/student data. A well-justified alternative may receive credit where it addresses changing requirements and close user participation.

Explain early delivery of working portions of the product.

questions.text: QUESTION 3.2 (6 marks): Calculate RETURN ON INVESTMENT (ROI) for BOTH projects using Table 1. Show your working.

questions.text: QUESTION 3.3 (6 marks): In which year does EACH project pay back its initial capital investment? Calculate the payback periods using Table 1, with working.
questions.correctAnswer: Project 1 cumulative unrecovered balance after years 1–3: −198 000+55 000+20 000+60 000 = −R63 000; year 4 brings R88 000. questions.text: QUESTION 3.4 (4 marks): Based on the results of 3.1–3.3, would you STILL recommend the project you selected in Question 1.1 for Tomorrow’s Future? Justify with the organisation’s CURRENT and FUTURE needs.
questions.correctAnswer: At the undiscounted level the payroll project has the greater net profit (R28 000 compared with R25 000), higher ROI (14.21% versus 12.63%), and marginally faster payback (3.57 versus 3.72 years). However, either the student or payroll system can be justified if the answer explains its urgency and strategic importance to Tomorrow’s Future, including the present dependence on St John University and long-term independence. Clearly state whether the original choice is retained and support the decision with both financial evidence and organisational needs.

questions.text: QUESTION 4.2 (4 marks): Based on your NPV calculations, advise Tomorrow’s Future which of the TWO projects to develop. Justify your answer.
questions.correctAnswer: At 10%, Project 2 (Salary/Payroll System) has the higher / less-negative NPV (about −R21 013.50 versus Project 1's −R26 289.50). Based strictly on the relative NPV comparison it is financially preferable if one must be chosen. Both NPVs are negative, however, so neither passes a stand-alone positive-NPV investment test; management should review the assumptions and consider essential strategic/operational benefits before committing. Credit a clear alternative recommendation that correctly explains the negative NPVs and organisational constraints.

questions.text: QUESTION 5.1 (14 marks): Draw an ACTIVITY-ON-ARROW (AOA) network for Table 3. Indicate the activity and duration on each arrow, and event number, earliest date, latest date and float on each node. Complete the forward and backward pass. IMPORTANT: The original paper deducts 7 of these 14 marks if there is no drawn network diagram. Draw in the box or upload a clear picture; optional text can explain your calculations.
questions.correctAnswer: A valid AOA solution (equivalent event numbering is accepted): node 1 is start (earliest/latest 0/0); arrows 1→2 A(7), 1→3 B(5), 1→5 F(11), 2→4 C(4), 3→4 D(5), 3→5 E(4), 4→6 H(3), 5→6 G(4). Node earliest/latest event dates: 1=0/0, 2=7/8, 3=5/7, 4=11/12, 5=11/11, 6=15/15. Event slack (latest−earliest): 0,1,2,1,0,0 respectively. Activity total floats: A=1, B=2, C=1, D=2, E=2, F=0, G=0, H=1. Project duration = 15 days. No dummy is required for this valid representation. Other correct event numbering and proper dummy arrangements also earn credit.
